newsitem.title: UK: RSI is still a workplace problem - medical journal.
newsitem.headline: RSI is still a workplace problem - medical journal.

text.p: Repetitive strain injury (RSI) has become an expensive problem for employers and health services, but quick and proper care prevents the worst complications, a Canadian expert said on Friday.
Although some employers say RSI is another name for malingering, Annalee Yassi of the University of Manitoba said the epidemic was real and had to be addressed.

The term repetitive strain injury (RSI) refers to any of several disorders affecting tendons, muscles, joints and nerves. They generally involve the back, neck, arms and hands and result from forced repetitive motions, awkward postures, and other problems of body position.
Conditions include tendonitis, carpal tunnel syndrome, arthritis and hand-arm vibration syndrome or Raynaud's syndrome.

Complaints about such disorders tripled in the United States between 1986 and 1993 and the number of worker's compensation claims allowed for them in the Canadian province of Ontario doubled between 1986 and 1991. U.S. compensation costs exceeded $20 billion a year.

RSI-type disorders accounted for more than 60 percent of industrial illnesses in the United States in 1990 with 1.9 million workers reporting symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome, a wrist disorder caused by a trapped nerve.
"More education in the workforce, and higher expectations as regards health, have changed worker tolerance for occupational aches and pains," Yassi wrote in a review for the Lancet medical journal.
But quick response eases most symptoms. Aspirin or similar drugs, cold packs and rest help. The best way to rest the affected limb was to change the work situation.
Yassi said it was important for employers to notice problem areas and change equipment if necessary.

"In one study in automobile manufacturers, for example, re-design of tools, fixtures and work organisation in assembly operations reduced the number of operations for carpal tunnel syndrome by 50 percent," she wrote.
Restricted duty, rest breaks and job rotation also helped, she said.
